EXPERIMENT 08
Steganography Detection and Quantitative Steganalysis Using StegExpose
Objective

To perform quantitative steganalysis and hidden payload detection in digital images using the StegExpose steganalysis tool, evaluate least significant bit (LSB) steganographic embedding, analyze fusion detection metrics across sample and controlled datasets, and verify evidence integrity.

Tools / Requirements
  • Forensic Tool: StegExpose Steganalysis Engine (Java-based, Version 1.0)
  • Image Processing: ImageMagick Utility Suite (magick)
  • Runtime Environment: Java Runtime Environment (JRE 17 / OpenJDK)
  • Host Operating System: Ubuntu Linux 24.04 LTS / Microsoft Windows 11
  • Datasets: Controlled Test Images (clean.png, test.png) and StegExpose Sample Benchmark Suite
Experiment Scenario
Controlled laboratory evidence was used for this experiment.

A steganalysis investigation was conducted to detect potential steganographic data concealment in digital image files. The examiner established baseline detection thresholds, prepared controlled baseline images, ran the StegExpose multi-algorithm detection engine (combining Primary Sets, Sample Pairs, Chi-Square, and RS Analysis), exported quantitative CSV reports, evaluated detection fusion scores, and verified evidence integrity via SHA-256 hashing.

Evidence / Input
  • Steganalysis Tool: StegExpose.jar (Multi-detector fusion engine)
  • Primary Evaluation Thresholds: Detection threshold 0.20, Min size 1000 bytes
  • Controlled Test Images: clean.png (872 bytes), test.png (872 bytes)
  • Benchmark Evaluation Suite: Standard sample dataset containing clean and steganographic carriers
  • Exported Evidence Reports: controlled_results.csv, sample_results.csv
Procedure
Step 1 — StegExpose Environment Inspection and Baseline Test

The StegExpose framework was launched with baseline parameters against the default test directory to verify multi-algorithm execution and reporting functionality.

Figure 8.1: StegExpose environment inspection and sample directory baseline run
Step 2 — Generation of Controlled Baseline Test Images

Controlled clean test images (clean.png and test.png) were synthesized using ImageMagick to serve as calibrated negative controls with known pristine pixel matrices.

Figure 8.2: Generation of controlled baseline test images
Step 3 — StegExpose Scan on Controlled Baseline Images

The command java -jar StegExpose.jar controlled_images/ 0.2 was executed. The analysis correctly returned false with 0% estimated payload, confirming pristine baseline integrity.

Figure 8.3: StegExpose scan against controlled baseline images
Step 4 — Structured CSV Export and Metric Analysis of Controlled Images

The steganalysis results for the controlled baseline were exported to CSV format, documenting detailed metrics: Primary Sets (0.0), Chi-Square (0.0), Sample Pairs (0.0), and RS Analysis (0.0).

Figure 8.4: Quantitative steganalysis CSV report for controlled images
Step 5 — Comparative Steganalysis on Benchmark Sample Dataset

A broader benchmark dataset containing steganographic carrier images was scanned. The multi-algorithm fusion engine identified positive steganographic indicators and estimated embedded payload sizes.

Figure 8.5: Steganalysis CSV report for benchmark sample dataset
Step 6 — Cryptographic Hash Auditing and Evidence Integrity Verification

The sha256sum utility was executed across all analyzed image files and generated CSV reports to establish cryptographic integrity records for the forensic examination.

Figure 8.6: Cryptographic SHA-256 verification of controlled and sample datasets
Step 7 — Single-Image StegExpose Analysis on the Controlled Baseline Images

Individual targeted image scans were conducted on clean.png and test.png to verify per-file metric stability and eliminate batch processing bias.

Figure 8.7: Single-image StegExpose evaluation on the controlled PNG images
Observations
  1. StegExpose executed successfully, combining Chi-Square, Primary Sets, Sample Pairs, and RS Analysis into an aggregated fusion metric.
  2. Controlled baseline test images yielded negative detection (false) with 0.0 fusion score, confirming the absence of hidden data.
  3. Benchmark dataset analysis detected hidden payloads in modified carriers with quantitative percentage estimates.
  4. Exported CSV reports provided verifiable metric logs for repeatable evidentiary auditing.
  5. SHA-256 hashing guaranteed forensic data authenticity throughout the steganalysis workflow.
Findings
  • Multi-Detector Fusion Accuracy: Combining four complementary LSB steganalysis methods significantly reduces false-positive rates compared to relying on single-metric statistical tests.
  • Quantitative Payload Estimation: StegExpose successfully estimated the embedded payload proportion in suspicious carrier images while accurately clearing pristine negative controls.
Conclusion

StegExpose provided robust quantitative steganalysis for detecting LSB-based hidden content in digital images. Controlled test images exhibited no steganographic markers, confirming baseline purity, while benchmark evaluation validated the effectiveness of multi-algorithm fusion detection.
